reason: The sources provide robust, multi-sourced details detailing UY Scuti's discovery, crowning in 2012, and subsequent downsizing via Gaia parallax measurements.
story: In 1860, German astronomers cataloged a dim dot in Scutum as BD-12°5055. Later named UY Scuti, this pulsating red supergiant stunned astronomers in 2012 when measurements from Chile's Very Large Telescope estimated its radius at an astounding 1,708 times that of the Sun. Crowned the largest star known in the universe, it was large enough to swallow the orbit of Jupiter and hold billions of Suns. However, stellar radius calculations depend directly on distance. The 2012 size assumed UY Scuti was roughly 9,500 light-years away. When the European Space Agency's Gaia mission delivered precise parallax measurements, astronomers discovered the star was actually much closer—around 5,900 light-years from Earth. Recalculated with this revised distance in 2023, UY Scuti's radius shrank to approximately 909 solar radii. While still a violent, pulsating behemoth destined for a supernova, the former cosmic titan was officially knocked off its throne.
angle: The undisputed largest star in the universe lost its cosmic crown overnight when a space telescope revealed it was thousands of light-years closer than previously thought—instantly slashing its calculated size in half.

claims.claim: UY Scuti was first cataloged in 1860 by German astronomers at the Bonn Observatory.
The star was originally designated BD-12°5055 in the Bonner Durchmusterung star catalog.
Following observed brightness variations, it was designated UY Scuti, denoting it as the 38th variable star identified in the constellation Scutum.
UY Scuti is located in the constellation Scutum.
The star is a pulsating semiregular variable star with a pulsation period of roughly 740 days.
In 2012, astronomers used the AMBER instrument on the Very Large Telescope in Chile's Atacama Desert to measure UY Scuti.
The 2012 study calculated UY Scuti's radius at approximately 1,708 solar radii.
The 1,708 solar radii estimate was based on an assumed distance of about 9,500 light-years.
Following the 2012 measurement, UY Scuti was widely crowned the largest known star in the universe.
At a radius of roughly 1,700 times the Sun, UY Scuti placed at the center of the Solar System would extend beyond the orbit of Jupiter.
A hypothetical object traveling at the speed of light would take about 7 hours to complete a circuit around UY Scuti, compared to 14.5 seconds for the Sun.
Measurements utilizing parallax data from the Gaia space telescope showed UY Scuti is closer than earlier assumed, at roughly 5,900 light-years.
With the updated Gaia distance, a 2023 study recalculated UY Scuti's radius down to roughly 909 solar radii.
Despite its immense physical volume, theoretical models estimate UY Scuti's mass at only 7 to 10 times that of the Sun.
UY Scuti loses mass at a rapid rate of 5.8 × 10^-5 solar masses per year, enveloping the star in an extensive cloud of gas and dust.
UY Scuti is currently fusing helium around its core and is expected to ultimately end its life in a core-collapse supernova.

disputed: Distance and radius values: Historical 2012 calculations placed it at 9,500 light-years and 1,708 solar radii, Gaia DR2 suggested 5,100 light-years and 755 solar radii, while Gaia DR3 calibrations place it at ~5,871–5,900 light-years and ~909 solar radii (or 1,100–1,200 solar radii according to another interpretation). The script should frame this as a scientific progression where improved distance estimates progressively reduced its calculated size.

Solar system reach: Sources describe UY Scuti reaching past Mars/asteroid belt (for 909 R☉), beyond Jupiter (for 1,700 R☉), or nearing Saturn. The script should explicitly link Jupiter reach to the older 1,708 R☉ estimate and Mars/asteroid belt reach to the newer 909 R☉ figure.

Earth visibility: S4 claims it can be viewed with binoculars, while S1 and S6 note its apparent magnitude of 8.29 to 10.56 makes it invisible to the naked eye and requires a small telescope. The script should avoid claiming naked-eye visibility.
